name: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) injury
populations: people with a previous wrist or distal radius injury
summary: Tear or wear of the cartilage-and-ligament complex on the ulnar side of the wrist, causing ulnar-sided pain, clicking and sometimes distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) instability. Traumatic or degenerative.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Nonoperative care is a reasonable first step: a systematic review of 8 studies (427 wrists) found outcomes comparable to surgery, but randomised trials are lacking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ulnar fovea sign: sensitivity 95.2% and specificity 86.5% in one arthroscopy series of 272 patients, but it also picks up ulnotriquetral tears; most TFCC tests are not validated against arthroscopy

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Pooled MRI sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81 for full-thickness tears versus 0.84 and 0.95 for MR arthrography (21 studies, 982 wrists)

keyFacts.label: Healing capacity
keyFacts.value: Only the peripheral 10–40% of the TFCC has a blood supply, so peripheral tears can heal or be repaired but central tears are unlikely to heal

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. In one small racquet-sport series the average return to baseline activity was 134 days

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Palmer class 1 (traumatic) and class 2 (degenerative); foveal tears matter because they threaten DRUJ stability

overview:
The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) is a composite structure on the ulnar side of the wrist made up of the articular disc, the dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments, the meniscus homologue, the ulnar collateral ligament and the sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU). Anatomical and biomechanical work showed that it acts as a cushion for the ulnar carpus and as a major stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) [r1]. Tears, acute or chronic, are a common cause of persistent ulnar-sided wrist pain [r2]. Palmer's classification separates traumatic lesions (class 1, grouped by location) from degenerative lesions (class 2, grouped by location and severity of wear in the TFCC, ulnar head, carpus and lunotriquetral ligament) [r3].

The foveal attachment of the radioulnar ligaments matters most for stability. The older picture of the TFCC as a hammock has been replaced by an iceberg model in which the submerged foveal insertions stabilise the DRUJ and ulnar carpus [r4], and the lamina fovealis is described as the most important restraining structure of the DRUJ [r5]. Where the tear lies also decides whether it can heal, because only the peripheral 10–40% of the complex has a blood supply [r6].

Diagnosis is hard. Provocative tests have only moderate accuracy, and most have not been checked against arthroscopy [r7,r8]. MRI is imperfect against arthroscopy, and MR arthrography is more accurate for full-thickness tears [r9]. Management is stepped. A systematic review of non-operatively treated traumatic tears found outcomes comparable to operative care, but it called for randomised trials [r10], and long-term comparative surgical studies are also limited [r2].

epidemiology.text:
Population incidence figures were not retrieved from the sources used for this page, so none are quoted. In a 9-year single-institution series of 700 patients diagnosed with a TFCC injury, 23.1% were injured during sport; 25 patients (15.4%) were playing a racquet sport, most commonly tennis (21 patients), and 75% of the included racquet-sport patients injured the dominant wrist [r11]. These figures come from a small retrospective chart review at one centre.

Structural change in the complex is common. In a dissection study of 61 wrists, 53% of specimens had a TFCC perforation, and every perforated wrist showed damage or erosion of the lunate and/or distal ulnar cartilage [r1]. The abstract does not state whether those wrists were symptomatic, so imaging and arthroscopic findings must be matched to the clinical picture (clinical reasoning).

intrinsic: Ulnar-positive variance, static or dynamic, which loads the ulnocarpal joint and is implicated in degenerative tears and ulnar impaction [r12]
Age and cumulative load: Palmer class 2 lesions are degenerative [r3], and age above 50 was associated with failure to return to baseline activity in one racquet-sport series [r11]
Previous TFCC pathology was associated with failure to return to baseline activity [r11]
Dominant hand: 75% of racquet-sport patients injured the dominant wrist [r11]
Previous distal radius or ulnar styloid injury altering the radioulnar relationship (clinical)
extrinsic: Fall on the outstretched hand with the forearm pronated, or a forced rotation or traction through a fixed hand (clinical)
Repetitive power grip with forearm rotation, for example golf, hockey and weightlifting (clinical)
Repetitive weight-bearing through the wrist, for example gymnastics and push-up based training (clinical)

mechanism.summary: Traumatic tears typically follow a fall on the outstretched hand with the forearm pronated, or a rotational or distraction force through a gripped hand, for example a racquet or club striking the ground (clinical; mechanism as commonly described). Axial load drives the ulnar head toward the carpus while rotation stresses the radioulnar ligaments at their foveal and peripheral attachments [r1,r4]. Degenerative tears arise from repeated ulnocarpal loading, often in an ulnar-positive wrist, which wears the central disc and then the lunate and ulnar head cartilage [r12,r13].
sequence: The hand is planted or gripped with the wrist extended and ulnar-deviated and the forearm pronated, for example in a fall or when a racquet or club hits the ground (clinical).
Axial load passes from the carpus into the ulnar head, and the TFCC acts as the cushion for the ulnar carpus [r1].
A rotational or distraction force on the fixed hand loads the dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments, which insert at the ulnar fovea and styloid [r4,r5].
The tear starts at the weakest point: the disc, the peripheral capsular attachment or the foveal insertion (Palmer class 1 by location [r3]).
A foveal disruption can weaken the DRUJ stabiliser, so the ulnar head may become unstable in the sigmoid notch [r4,r14].
Pain is felt over the ulnar fovea and on loaded rotation or ulnar deviation, often with clicking (clinical; ulnar fovea tenderness [r14]).
Peripheral tears have a blood supply and can heal or be repaired, but central and radial-side tears are unlikely to heal [r6].
With ongoing ulnocarpal loading, the disc perforates and the lunate and ulnar head cartilage erode (Palmer class 2, ulnar impaction) [r1,r12].

variants.name: Traumatic tear (Palmer class 1)
variants.description: Acute lesion from a fall, rotation or distraction; classified by location (central, ulnar-side peripheral, distal or radial-side) [r3].

variants.name: Foveal tear with DRUJ instability
variants.description: Disruption of the foveal insertion of the radioulnar ligaments; typically associated with an unstable DRUJ, whereas ulnotriquetral ligament tears are typically associated with a stable DRUJ [r14,r4].

variants.name: Degenerative tear and ulnar impaction (Palmer class 2)
variants.description: Progressive wear from repeated ulnocarpal loading, with disc thinning, perforation and chondromalacia of the lunate and ulnar head; ulnar-positive variance plays a role [r12,r13].

variants.name: Racquet-sport TFCC injury
variants.description: Tennis was the most common racquet sport in a retrospective series; most patients were treated non-operatively [r11].

anatomy.text: The TFCC lies between the ulnar head and the proximal carpal row (lunate and triquetrum). It is not a single structure: dissection shows an articular disc, the dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments, the meniscus homologue, the ulnar collateral ligament and the ECU sheath, which cannot be separated into independent parts [r1]. The radioulnar ligaments insert on the ulna at the styloid (superficial) and the fovea (deep) (textbook anatomy), and the lamina fovealis, the deep continuation of the radioulnar ligaments at their ulnar insertion, is described as the most important restraint of the DRUJ [r5]. Small vessels penetrate the periphery from the palmar, ulnar and dorsal capsular attachments and supply the peripheral 10–40%; the inner disc is avascular and no vessels cross the radial attachment [r6].

structures.name: Articular disc (central)
structures.role: Cushions the ulnar carpus and transmits load between the carpus and the ulna; the avascular central zone [r1,r6]

structures.name: Dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments
structures.role: Stabilise the DRUJ through forearm rotation and bind the disc to the radius [r1,r5]

structures.name: Foveal attachment (lamina fovealis)
structures.role: Deep insertion of the radioulnar ligaments at the ulnar fovea; the key DRUJ restraint [r5,r4]

structures.name: Meniscus homologue and ulnocarpal ligaments
structures.role: Part of the ulnar-side capsule linking the TFCC to the triquetrum and lunate [r1,r5]

structures.name: ECU subsheath
structures.role: Forms part of the TFCC complex on the ulnar-dorsal side; links TFCC and ECU problems [r1]

structures.name: Ulnar head, styloid and fovea
structures.role: Bony origin for the radioulnar ligaments; the fovea is the site of tenderness in the ulnar fovea sign [r14]

structures.name: Lunate and triquetrum
structures.role: Carpal bones loaded against the disc; cartilage erosion here follows disc perforation [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In a traumatic tear the force exceeds the capacity of the disc or of its peripheral and foveal attachments. Where the tear sits shapes both the clinical picture and the healing potential: peripheral tears lie in the zone supplied by capsular vessels and may mount a reparative response, whereas central tears and tears at the radial attachment do not have immediate access to a blood supply and are unlikely to heal [r6]. Foveal tears matter because the foveal insertion is the main stabiliser of the DRUJ and ulnar carpus [r4,r5].

In degenerative disease the disc thins and perforates under repeated ulnocarpal load, and the lunate and ulnar head cartilage erode; Palmer class 2 grades this by location and severity of wear in the TFCC, ulnar head, carpus and lunotriquetral ligament [r3,r1]. Painful degeneration is called ulnar impaction, and bone marrow oedema in the ulnar head or the proximal ulnar lunate can support the diagnosis on MRI [r13]. Excising the whole complex may lead to ulnolunate abutment, chronic pain or DRUJ instability, which is why it is not recommended [r1].

structures.name: Articular disc
structures.effect: Central tear or perforation, often degenerative; avascular so it does not heal [r6,r12]

structures.name: Radioulnar ligaments at the fovea
structures.effect: Foveal avulsion or tear can destabilise the DRUJ [r4,r14]

structures.name: Peripheral capsular attachment
structures.effect: Peripheral ulnar-side tear with a blood supply that can support repair or healing [r6,r15]

structures.name: Ulnotriquetral ligament
structures.effect: Commonly injured alongside foveal lesions and gives a similar positive fovea sign, typically with a stable DRUJ [r14]

structures.name: Lunate and ulnar head cartilage
structures.effect: Chondromalacia and marrow oedema in ulnar impaction [r1,r13]

muscles.name: Pronator quadratus and ECU
muscles.effect: Dynamic DRUJ and ulnar-side stabilisers; their training is the rationale for conservative rehabilitation, but no trial of this was retrieved (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Forearm rotators and wrist flexors and extensors
muscles.effect: Pain-related inhibition limits grip and rotation strength; guarding follows loaded rotation (clinical).

muscles.name: Intrinsic and finger flexors
muscles.effect: Grip is reduced by pain; grip strength improved after treatment in a foveal-sign audit [r16].

cellular.description: Tear with local haemorrhage and a synovitis in the radiocarpal and ulnocarpal joint (clinical).
Vessels from the capsular attachments support a reparative response in the peripheral zone [r6].

cellular.phase: No repair in the avascular zone
cellular.description: Central and radial-side tears have no immediate blood supply and are unlikely to heal, so symptoms depend on instability, synovitis and load [r6].
Disc thinning and perforation, then chondromalacia of the lunate and ulnar head [r1,r12].

systems.effect: Local ulnar-sided pain is amplified by loaded rotation; persistent pain after surgery is a recognised outcome (clinical).
DRUJ instability alters forearm rotation mechanics; ulnar-positive variance changes ulnocarpal load [r12].
Ulnocarpal synovitis and cartilage erosion drive mechanical pain and clicking [r1].
Racquet-sport and grip-dependent work make loading hard to avoid; return to baseline activity took an average 134 days in one series [r11].

grading.system: Palmer classification (traumatic class 1, degenerative class 2). Sub-class descriptions follow the classic scheme and are not drawn from a single abstract read

grades.description: Central perforation of the articular disc.
grades.prognosis: The central disc is avascular and unlikely to heal [r6]; often managed by debridement, with residual symptoms in as many as 25% after debridement alone in one review [r12]

grades.description: Peripheral ulnar-side avulsion, with or without an ulnar styloid fracture; may involve the foveal attachment and DRUJ stability.
grades.prognosis: A short period of above-elbow immobilisation was effective in a systematic review; DRUJ subluxation and full foveal tears were risk factors for poor outcome or surgery [r10]

grades.description: Distal avulsion from the lunate or triquetrum (ulnocarpal ligament injury).
grades.prognosis: Ulnotriquetral ligament injuries also give a positive ulnar fovea sign, typically with a stable DRUJ [r14]

grades.description: Radial-side avulsion from the sigmoid notch.
grades.prognosis: No vessels cross the radial attachment, so healing is unlikely [r6]

grades.description: Progressive wear: disc thinning (2A), plus lunate or ulnar head chondromalacia (2B), plus disc perforation (2C), plus lunotriquetral ligament perforation (2D), plus ulnocarpal arthritis (2E).
grades.prognosis: Often linked to ulnar-positive variance; options include debridement with wafer resection or ulnar shortening if conservative care fails [r3,r12,r13]

timeframes.summary: There is no validated healing timeline. The phases below combine tissue biology (peripheral vascular repair only) with common clinical conventions, and criteria override time. In one small racquet-sport series, the average return to baseline activity was 134 days [r11].

healing.description: A short period of above-elbow immobilisation was effective in Palmer 1B tears; the duration was not stated in the abstract, and 4–6 weeks is a common clinical convention [r10]
Only the peripheral 10–40% has a blood supply; central and radial-side tears are unlikely to heal [r6]

healing.phase: Restore motion and rebuild load tolerance
healing.description: Progressive range, grip and forearm strength once symptoms allow (clinical)

healing.phase: Return to sport and full loading
healing.description: Graded exposure to grip, rotation and weight-bearing; average return to baseline activity was 134 days in a racquet-sport series [r11]

milestones.label: Begin active wrist motion (if non-operative and settled)
milestones.note: A common clinical convention after a short period of immobilisation; surgeon's protocol overrides after repair

milestones.label: Review of non-operative response
milestones.note: A 3-month trial before discussing surgery is a common clinical convention; there is no randomised trial to define it [r10]

milestones.label: Mean return to baseline activity in racquet players
milestones.note: Retrospective series; age above 50 and previous TFCC pathology were associated with no return [r11]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based rather than time-based. A common clinical range is about 3 to 6 months for non-operative or arthroscopic care in athletes (one racquet-sport series: average 134 days [r11]) and longer after foveal repair or reconstruction, following the surgeon's protocol.

symptoms: Ulnar-sided wrist pain, worse with loaded forearm rotation, gripping, push-up type weight-bearing and ulnar deviation
Clicking, catching or a feeling of instability on the ulnar side of the wrist
A fall on the outstretched hand or a rotational or traction injury (traumatic), or insidious onset in an older or ulnar-positive wrist (degenerative)
Reduced grip strength because of pain
Pain when turning a door handle, key or jar lid, or when swinging a racquet or club
signs: Tenderness at the ulnar fovea, between the ulnar styloid and the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon [r14]
Pain with ulnar deviation and axial loading of the wrist (ulnocarpal stress), with or without a click
Painful or reduced forearm rotation; a DRUJ that translates more than the other side on dorsopalmar stress (clinical)
Reduced grip strength compared with the other hand
Mild ulnar-sided swelling after acute injury (clinical)

subjective: Mechanism: fall on the outstretched pronated hand, rotational or traction injury, or insidious onset [r11]
Site and behaviour of pain: ulnar fovea, ulnar-dorsal or ulnocarpal; aggravated by rotation, grip and loaded ulnar deviation
Clicking, clunking or instability when turning the forearm
Sport and work demands: racquet grip, weight-bearing and rotational loads
Previous wrist injury, distal radius fracture or surgery, and previous treatment and response
Night pain, numbness in the ulnar border of the hand or systemic symptoms (to exclude other causes)
observation: Prominence of the ulnar head or an abnormal resting forearm position
palpation: Ulnar fovea, between the ulnar styloid and flexor carpi ulnaris (tenderness suggests foveal disruption or ulnotriquetral injury [r14])
Ulnar styloid, ulnocarpal joint line and triquetrum
ECU tendon in its groove (separate ECU pathology)
Hook of hamate, pisiform and lunotriquetral interval to separate differentials
rangeOfMotion: Forearm pronation and supination (end-range pain or a block)
Wrist flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation
strength: Grip dynamometry compared with the other hand
Resisted wrist extension and ulnar deviation (ECU) to separate ECU pathology
neuro: Sensation over the dorsal and palmar ulnar border of the hand (dorsal ulnar sensory branch and ulnar nerve)
Screen C8 and the cervical spine if symptoms are not local
functional: Observe a racquet grip, push-up or weight-bearing task and loaded rotation
Timed functional tasks such as turning a door handle or opening a jar (patient-specific)

specialTests.name: Ulnar fovea sign
specialTests.purpose: Detect foveal disruption of the radioulnar ligaments and ulnotriquetral ligament injury
specialTests.procedure: The examiner presses a thumb distally into the interval between the ulnar styloid and flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, between the volar surface of the ulnar head and the pisiform, and compares with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Exquisite tenderness that reproduces the patient's pain. It does not separate foveal disruption from ulnotriquetral tears; the latter typically occur with a stable DRUJ [r14].
specialTests.sensitivity: 95.2% for foveal disruption and/or ulnotriquetral injury

specialTests.name: Pisiform boost test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain from a TFCC tear by loading the ulnar carpus in ulnar deviation
specialTests.procedure: Assess ulnar fovea pain with passive ulnar deviation of the wrist, then repeat with digital pressure over the pisiform.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of ulnar-sided pain. In a retrospective series of 82 wrists the sensitivity was high and the specificity low (similar to the ulnar grinding test), so the authors advised combining it with other tests [r17].

specialTests.name: Ulnocarpal stress (ulnar grinding) test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke ulnocarpal pain or click from disc or ulnar impaction pathology
specialTests.procedure: Axially load the ulnarly deviated wrist while passively rotating the forearm.
specialTests.positive: Pain or a click over the ulnar wrist. Accuracy figures for this test alone were not retrieved; one study described its specificity as similar to that of the pisiform boost test (0.33) [r17].

specialTests.name: Press test and DRUJ dorsopalmar stress test
specialTests.purpose: Assess DRUJ stability and foveal incompetence
specialTests.procedure: Press test: the patient pushes up from a chair using both hands, and ulnar-sided pain is noted. Dorsopalmar stress: translate the ulnar head dorsally and volarly against the radius with the wrist and forearm stabilised, and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Ulnar-sided pain on pressing, or increased translation and a soft end-feel compared with the other side. The ulnar fovea sign, dorsopalmar stress test and press test were described as the most reliable DRUJ tests, but most tests have not been evaluated against arthroscopy and accuracy figures were not retrieved [r8].

clinicalRules.name: Combine tests; none is diagnostic alone
clinicalRules.description: A systematic review found that physical examination for TFCC lesions had sensitivity 58–90%, specificity 20–69% and accuracy 56–73% across studies, so no single provocation test confirms or excludes a tear [r7]. Pair focal fovea tenderness with the mechanism, DRUJ stability, imaging and exclusion of fracture and other ulnar-sided causes.

clinicalRules.name: Match imaging to the clinical picture
clinicalRules.description: Structural TFCC change is common in dissection (perforation in 53% of 61 wrists [r1]), so an MRI finding does not prove it is the pain source (clinical reasoning).

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE)
outcomeMeasures.use: Wrist pain and function; a common patient-reported outcome in wrist surgery research (clinical)

outcomeMeasures.name: DASH or QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Upper-limb disability; DASH improved from 41 to 6 after foveal repair in a cohort of 44 [r18]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain VAS or NPRS
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at rest and with grip; VAS fell from 63 to 14 after foveal repair in the same cohort [r18]

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength compared with the other side; grip rose from 29 to 36 kgf after foveal repair [r18]

imaging.modality: Plain radiographs (PA, lateral, with a neutral-rotation PA for ulnar variance)
imaging.indication: All ulnar-sided wrist pain; exclude fracture and measure ulnar variance
imaging.findings: Ulnar variance, ulnar styloid fracture, DRUJ malalignment and arthrosis; stress views can show ulnocarpal narrowing under load [r13]

imaging.indication: Persistent pain after a trial of conservative care, or suspected instability or associated injury
imaging.findings: Pooled sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81 for full-thickness tears against arthroscopy; insufficient data for partial tears [r9]. TFCC accuracy 89–91% at 3 T in a systematic review [r7]. Bone marrow oedema in the ulnar head or lunate suggests ulnar impaction [r13].

imaging.indication: When MRI is equivocal and the result will change management
imaging.findings: MR arthrography was more accurate than MRI for full-thickness tears (sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.95) [r9]; MR and CT arthrography are described as the reference standard in imaging [r5].

imaging.indication: Persistent symptoms with a diagnostic question or a planned repair, debridement or wafer procedure
imaging.findings: The reference standard for TFCC lesions; it confirms and treats, but it is invasive and not a screening test [r7,r9].

differentials.name: Scapholunate ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Dorsal-radial wrist pain, positive scaphoid shift test and a widened scapholunate interval on a clenched-fist view; not fovea tenderness.

differentials.name: ECU tendinopathy or subluxation
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness over the ECU groove, pain on resisted ulnar deviation and, in subluxation, a palpable snap on supination and ulnar deviation.

differentials.name: Hook of hamate fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness over the hook, pain on gripping a club or racquet and a positive hook pull test; image with CT.

differentials.name: Distal radius or ulnar styloid fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Trauma with focal bony tenderness and swelling; image first and note that TFCC injury can coexist.

differentials.name: Ulnar tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Numbness and weakness in the ulnar nerve distribution with a Tinel sign at Guyon's canal.

differentials.name: Lunotriquetral ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the lunotriquetral interval with a positive shear or ballottement test; commonly considered alongside ulnar-sided pain.

differentials.name: Triquetral fracture, pisotriquetral arthritis or DRUJ arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness, radiographic findings or a grind test; triquetral fractures should be in the differential for ulnar-sided pain after a fall on the outstretched hand, and TFCC injury is a recognised accompanying injury [r19].

differentials.name: Kienböck's disease (lunate osteonecrosis)
differentials.distinguishing: Central dorsal wrist pain and stiffness; sclerosis or collapse of the lunate on radiographs or MRI.

redFlags: Locked or dislocated DRUJ (fixed forearm rotation, a prominent or irreducible ulnar head): urgent hand surgery review.

Acute wrist trauma with focal bony tenderness (hook of hamate, triquetrum, scaphoid, distal radius) or a normal-looking X-ray with persistent pain: image with CT or MRI and treat as a fracture until excluded.
Large ulnar styloid base fracture with DRUJ instability after a fall: refer to hand surgery, because it can affect foveal stability (clinical).
Hot, red, swollen wrist with fever, or a penetrating wound: suspect septic arthritis or infection; refer to emergency.
Progressive numbness, weakness or clawing in the ulnar nerve distribution: arrange urgent assessment for nerve compression.

Persistent pain and mechanical symptoms despite a well-delivered conservative program, especially with foveal tenderness or DRUJ instability: refer to hand surgery, since DRUJ subluxation and full foveal tears were risk factors for failure of non-operative care [r10].

management.principles: Management is stepped and shared with the patient. A systematic review of 8 studies (425 patients) of non-operatively treated traumatic tears found outcomes noninferior and comparable to operative management, and that Palmer 1B tears treated with a short period of above-elbow immobilisation did well; risk factors for a poor outcome or for needing surgery were DRUJ subluxation, short-arm immobilisation and full tears of the foveal attachment, and randomised trials with homogeneous data are still needed [r10]. Surgery is considered when a well-delivered conservative program fails or when foveal disruption with an unstable DRUJ is confirmed [r4,r15]. Operative options (debridement, wafer resection, repair, reconstruction) have only limited comparative evidence [r2]. Excising the whole complex is not recommended [r1].

medical.name: Immobilisation (above-elbow or long-arm splint) for a short period in traumatic Palmer 1B tears
medical.description: A short period of above-elbow immobilisation was an effective option with good functional scores in a systematic review of non-operative care; short-arm immobilisation was a risk factor for poor outcome. The abstract does not state the duration, so 4–6 weeks is a common clinical convention only [r10].

medical.name: Analgesia, NSAIDs or corticosteroid injection for symptom control
medical.description: Commonly used to settle pain so that rehabilitation can proceed. No trial or review evidence for these options in TFCC injury was retrieved for this page, so they are listed as clinical practice only.

medical.name: Arthroscopic debridement of central tears and wafer resection or ulnar shortening for ulnar impaction
medical.description: Residual symptoms persisted in as many as 25% of wrists after debridement alone in one review, and combined debridement with wafer resection was feasible for ulnar impaction [r12]. Ulnar shortening osteotomy or wafer resection follows when conservative treatment fails [r13].

medical.name: Arthroscopic or open repair of peripheral and foveal tears
medical.description: Reattachment gave good to excellent results in 60–90% of cases in one review of arthroscopic repair [r15]. In a prospective cohort of 44 patients, VAS fell from 63 to 14 and DASH from 41 to 6 at a mean of 31 months, all achieved stability, and 6 needed re-operation (3 for renewed injury) [r18]. Comparative long-term data are limited [r2].

medical.name: Complete excision of the TFCC
medical.description: Anatomical and biomechanical work advised against excising the whole complex because it may lead to ulnolunate abutment, chronic wrist pain or DRUJ instability [r1].

physio.name: Education, load modification and activity pacing
physio.description: Explain that ulnar-sided pain has several causes, that imaging findings are common, and that many people improve without surgery [r10]. Modify loaded rotation, grip size and weight-bearing; adjust racquet grip and swing volume (clinical).

physio.name: Splinting or bracing to offload the ulnar wrist
physio.description: If immobilising, discuss above-elbow rather than short-arm immobilisation for traumatic tears, because short-arm immobilisation was a risk factor for poor outcome in the review [r10]. A wrist or ulnar-side support for activity is a common clinical option with no trial evidence retrieved.

physio.name: Progressive exercise: range, grip, forearm rotation and ulnar-side stabiliser strength
physio.description: Graded loading of grip, pronation and supination, ECU and pronator quadratus after the irritable phase, then graded weight-bearing (see rehab stages). No randomised trial of a specific physiotherapy program for TFCC injury was retrieved; the dosages are common clinical conventions.

physio.name: Aggressive early stretching or loaded end-range rotation or ulnar deviation
physio.description: Forcing end-range rotation or compressive ulnar deviation under load early can reproduce pain and stress a healing foveal or peripheral tear. This is clinical reasoning; no comparative data were retrieved.

education: The TFCC is a cushion and stabiliser on the little-finger side of the wrist. Tears and wear are common and do not always explain pain, so treatment is guided by your symptoms and function as much as by the scan.
Many people do well without surgery in the studies reviewed, but if the forearm is unstable, pain persists or the tear is at the foveal attachment, a surgical opinion is reasonable [r10].
Pain with twisting and weight-bearing is expected early. Avoid forcing painful end-range rotation or ulnar deviation, and build grip and forearm strength gradually.

Central tears are unlikely to heal because that part of the disc has no blood supply [r6]. Many people still improve with load management and rehabilitation, but this was not tested directly in the studies reviewed.
If you play racquet sports, expect a graded return over several months rather than weeks (an average of 134 days in one small series) [r11].

rehab.overview: This program applies to non-operative care and to arthroscopic debridement. After foveal repair or reconstruction the surgeon's protocol (immobilisation, rotation limits, scar care) overrides it. No randomised trial of a physiotherapy program for TFCC injury was retrieved, so the stages are criteria-based, the dosages are common clinical conventions, and progression follows symptoms, DRUJ stability and strength rather than the calendar. The aims are to settle irritability, restore forearm rotation and wrist range, rebuild grip and ulnar-side stabiliser strength, then re-introduce weight-bearing and sport loads.

stages.name: Protect & settle
goals: Protect the injured TFCC from loaded rotation and compression
Keep the shoulder, elbow and fingers moving
precautions: No forceful rotation, compressive ulnar deviation or weight-bearing through the wrist
Follow the splint or immobilisation type and duration prescribed (above-elbow immobilisation was reported for traumatic 1B tears [r10])
Refer if the DRUJ is unstable or locked

exercises.name: Splint wear schedule
exercises.dosage: Wear as prescribed, removing it for hygiene and gentle range (a common convention is 4–6 weeks for traumatic tears)
exercises.cues: Fit to support the forearm and wrist; check skin and swelling

exercises.name: Active finger, thumb, elbow and shoulder range
exercises.cues: Keep the wrist still; avoid stiffness elsewhere

exercises.name: Elevation and gentle finger pumping for swelling
exercises.cues: Hand above heart level

exercises.name: Pain-free active wrist flexion and extension (when cleared)
exercises.cues: Forearm supported and neutral; stop at first pain

exercises.name: Submaximal pain-free grip
exercises.dosage: 10 × 5 s holds at low effort, daily
exercises.cues: Wrist neutral; no pain on gripping

progressionCriteria: Cleared by the treating clinician to start active rotation

stages.name: Restore motion & early loading
goals: Restore pain-free forearm rotation and wrist range
Start isometric then light isotonic loading
precautions: Keep pain no higher than 3–4/10 during loading and settled within 24 hours
Avoid end-range loaded rotation and ulnar deviation
Stop and review if clicking, instability or night pain increase

exercises.name: Active pronation and supination, elbow at 90°
exercises.cues: Slow and controlled; stay within the pain-free range

exercises.name: Active wrist flexion, extension and radial deviation
exercises.cues: Progress range by about 10° as comfort allows

exercises.name: Isometric wrist extension and flexion (neutral)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s holds, 1–2 times daily (a common convention)
exercises.cues: Moderate effort; pain 3/10 or less

exercises.name: Putty or soft ball grip
exercises.cues: Wrist neutral; avoid ulnar deviation under load

exercises.name: Isometric pronation and supination with a band or towel
exercises.cues: Forearm supported at the elbow; keep the DRUJ comfortable

progressionCriteria: Forearm rotation within 10° of the other side without pain
Grip at least 60–70% of the other side (a common convention)
No DRUJ clunk or giving way

stages.name: Strength & stabiliser control
goals: Strengthen ECU and pronator quadratus as dynamic ulnar-side stabilisers
Introduce graded weight-bearing through the wrist
Tolerate sustained work and sport tasks
precautions: Add load gradually, no faster than symptoms and DRUJ stability allow
Introduce weight-bearing on the heel of the hand first and progress slowly
Persisting clicking or instability warrants review

exercises.name: Forearm pronation and supination with a hammer or weighted bar
exercises.cues: Elbow at the side; control the end of range

exercises.name: Wrist extension, flexion and ulnar deviation with a dumbbell
exercises.cues: Forearm supported; slow lowering

exercises.name: Grip and pinch strengthening (putty or gripper)
exercises.cues: Progress resistance as pain stays settled

exercises.name: Quadruped weight-bearing shifts
exercises.cues: Hands under shoulders; start with fingers turned out if neutral hurts

exercises.name: Incline push-up
exercises.cues: Even load through both hands; stay pain-free

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.cues: Neutral wrists, tall posture

progressionCriteria: Grip at least 85–90% of the other side (a common convention)
Pain 2/10 or less after loading sessions
Negative or minimally painful provocation tests

stages.name: Return to sport & prevention
goals: Return to full sport, work and grip tasks
Restore sport-specific power and rotation control
precautions: Increase racquet, club or weight-bearing volume gradually
Re-refer if clicking, instability or night pain return

exercises.name: Sport-specific loading (racquet, club or stick)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 50% of usual volume and add 10–20% per week (common convention)
exercises.cues: Begin with controlled strokes before power

exercises.name: Rotational power with a light medicine ball or weighted implement
exercises.cues: Maintain neutral wrists and a controlled grip

exercises.name: Plyometric hand loading (wall or bench push-aways)
exercises.cues: Land with even load; progress only if pain-free

exercises.name: Heavy grip and wrist maintenance
exercises.cues: Symptom-guided progression

progressionCriteria: Full training load without a flare
Grip at least 90% of the other side
Provocation tests negative or minimally painful
Patient has a plan for load management and early recurrence

criteria: Pain-free daily tasks with full or near-full forearm rotation and wrist range
Grip strength at about 90% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
No DRUJ clunk, instability or locking with rotation and weight-bearing
Negative or minimally painful ulnar fovea, ulnocarpal stress and press tests
Tolerates graded sport-specific grip, swing and weight-bearing loads without a flare
Surgical protocol completed and cleared by the surgeon if repair or reconstruction was performed
tests: Grip dynamometry compared with the other side
Pain NPRS or VAS during sport-specific tasks
Provocation tests (ulnar fovea sign, ulnocarpal stress, press test)

prognosis: Many traumatic tears improve without surgery, but evidence is limited. A systematic review of 8 studies found outcomes of non-operative care comparable to operative care, with DRUJ subluxation, short-arm immobilisation and full foveal tears as risk factors for poor outcome or surgery [r10]. In a retrospective audit of 100 wrists with a positive ulnar fovea sign, 54% managed non-surgically and 83% managed surgically reported pain improvement, and wrists with an unstable DRUJ had better pain outcomes, but the groups were not randomised [r16]. After arthroscopic foveal reattachment, 60–90% good to excellent results were reported in one review [r15], and in a 44-patient cohort 6 needed re-operation [r18]. In a small racquet-sport series (20 included patients, so treat as indicative only, and the abstract's counts and percentage are not fully consistent) non-operative care resolved in 73.3% and all surgical patients returned; age above 50 and previous TFCC pathology were associated with no return to baseline activity [r11]. Central tears are unlikely to heal [r6]; whether pain settles regardless is clinical experience and was not tested in the sources retrieved.
prevention: Build forearm rotation, grip and ulnar-side stabiliser strength before increasing racquet, club or weight-bearing load (clinical).
Increase repetitive weight-bearing and rotational loads gradually (clinical).
Check grip size, racquet weight and technique, particularly in tennis, which was the most common racquet sport in one series [r11].
Teach safe falling technique where relevant; no trial evidence was retrieved (clinical).
Review ulnar variance if ulnar-sided pain recurs with repetitive loading [r12].
clinicalPearls: A positive ulnar fovea sign is sensitive (95.2% in one series) but cannot tell a foveal tear from an ulnotriquetral tear, and the DRUJ is typically stable in the latter [r14].
Treat provocation tests as a group: sensitivity and specificity ranged widely across studies (58–90% and 20–69%), and the pisiform boost test had a specificity of only 33% [r7,r17].
MRI misses and over-calls TFCC lesions; MR arthrography is more accurate for full-thickness tears, and arthroscopy remains the reference [r9].

Always check DRUJ stability against the other side before choosing short-arm immobilisation: DRUJ subluxation and short-arm immobilisation were both risk factors for failure of non-operative care [r10].
Ulnar-positive variance changes the diagnosis from an acute tear to ulnar impaction and changes the surgical options [r12,r13].
Do not assume a central tear needs surgery: it is unlikely to heal, but symptoms depend on load and DRUJ stability (clinical), whereas peripheral and foveal tears have a repair option [r6,r15].

forces.label: Axial load with the forearm pronated

captions.text: A tennis player lunges for a wide ball.
She stumbles and puts the right hand out to break the fall.
The palm lands with the wrist extended and the forearm pronated.
Axial load drives the ulnar head toward the carpus while the forearm twists.
The ulnar side of the wrist is painful, and the forearm may feel unstable.
Zooming into the right wrist, viewed from the palm side.

actions.label: Axial load through the ulnar carpus

actions.text: Traumatic (class 1) tear at the ulnar attachment
Class 2: degenerative wear and ulnar impaction

captions.text: The TFCC sits between the ulnar head and the carpus on the little-finger side.
Axial load squeezes the disc between the lunate and the ulna.
Rotation tears the peripheral and foveal attachment, which can destabilise the DRUJ.
Pain is felt over the ulnar fovea; the ulnar fovea sign is positive.
In the degenerative pattern the central disc wears and perforates over years.
The lunate and ulnar head then bruise and erode: ulnar impaction.
Healthy fibrocartilage: collagen bundles aligned to resist compression and tension.
Axial and rotational load strains the fibres (schematic: the meniscus model stands in for the TFCC disc).
The fibres fail where the load is greatest.
The outer 10–40% has a blood supply, so a peripheral tear can mount a repair response.
The inner disc is avascular: a central tear is unlikely to heal, so symptoms depend on load and stability.
